questions.question: Describe the patterns of colonisation in Africa, including types of colony and methods of rule.
questions.expected_answer: Colonisation usually began on the coast, at existing trading posts, forts and harbours, and moved inland along rivers, trade routes and railways: in West Africa from Senegal, the Gambia, Sierra Leone, the Gold Coast and Lagos along the Niger and Senegal; in Central Africa along the Congo; in East Africa from the Indian Ocean coast along caravan routes and later railways such as the Uganda Railway, completed to Lake Victoria in 1901; north from the Cape and Natal; and from Algeria and Egypt in the north. Settler colonies such as Algeria, South Africa, Southern Rhodesia and Kenya attracted many Europeans who took the best land; non-settler colonies such as Nigeria and the Gold Coast had few settlers and Africans farmed for export; protectorates kept existing rulers under colonial control. The British often used indirect rule through African rulers, as with the emirs of northern Nigeria, while the French used direct rule and assimilation, though few Africans got citizenship. Centralised kingdoms often resisted long, while divided societies were taken faster but were harder to control.

questions.question: Explain why European powers were able to colonise Africa so quickly.
questions.expected_answer: European armies had breech-loading rifles, artillery, armed steamboats and from the 1880s the Maxim gun, while many African armies had older guns or spears and Europeans restricted arms sales, so small forces defeated large armies, as at Omdurman in 1898. Quinine reduced malaria deaths, and steamships, railways and the telegraph moved troops and information quickly. Most colonial soldiers were Africans, such as Senegalese riflemen, the West African Frontier Force and the askari, and Europeans allied with African rulers. Rivalries between and within African states allowed divide and rule. Treaties gave claims other powers recognised, and chartered companies such as the Royal Niger Company and the British South Africa Company raised private armies. Drought, famine and especially rinderpest in the 1890s, which killed huge numbers of cattle, weakened many societies. The Berlin agreements kept European powers from fighting each other, while African states had no such agreement. The combination, not one factor, explains the speed.

questions.question: Describe African resistance to colonisation, explaining why Ethiopia succeeded.
questions.expected_answer: Africans resisted everywhere through war, diplomacy, rebellion, refusal of taxes and labour, migration and religious movements. Samori Touré resisted the French from the early 1880s to 1898 with a modern-armed army; the Asante fought the British repeatedly; the Mahdist state defeated Gordon at Khartoum in 1885 and ruled until Omdurman in 1898; the Zulu won at Isandlwana in 1879; and the Ndebele and Shona rose in 1896 to 1897. Rebellions after conquest included the Herero and Nama risings from 1904, crushed with an extermination order, deaths in the desert and camps, recognised as genocide, the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 to 1907 against forced cotton growing, crushed with famine, and the Bambatha Rebellion of 1906. Ethiopia succeeded because Menelik II unified the country, built a large army, bought modern rifles and artillery, and fought on known ground, defeating Italy at Adwa on 1 March 1896, which forced Italy to recognise Ethiopian independence and made Adwa a symbol of African resistance.
